baseline.answer: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on large amounts of text to predict the next token in a sequence. Through this training, it learns patterns in language, grammar, and facts represented in its training data.

How Large Language Models Work
1. What Is a Large Language Model
A Large Language Model (LLM) is a type of neural network trained on massive amounts of text data
to predict the next word, or more precisely the next token, in a sequence. Despite this relatively
simple training objective, LLMs learn to capture grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and even some
limited problem-solving ability purely from statistical patterns in the training data.
Modern LLMs are built on the Transformer architecture, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All
You Need'. The Transformer replaced earlier recurrent architectures like RNNs and LSTMs with a
mechanism called self-attention, which allows the model to weigh the relevance of every other token
in a sequence when processing a given token, regardless of distance between them.
2. Tokenization
Before text can be processed by an LLM, it must be converted into tokens, which are numerical

LLMs are typically trained in multiple stages. The first stage, pretraining, involves training the model
on a very large, diverse corpus of text using the next-token prediction objective. This stage requires
enormous computational resources and is where the model acquires most of its general knowledge
and language ability.
The second stage, often called fine-tuning or instruction tuning, involves further training the model on
smaller, curated datasets of instructions and desired responses, teaching the model to follow user
instructions more reliably.
A third stage, commonly Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), uses human
preference data to further align model outputs with what humans consider helpful, honest, and
harmless, by training a reward model and using it to fine-tune the LLM's behavior.
5. Inference and Generation
During inference, the model generates text one token at a time. At each step, it produces a probability

Tokenization and Text Preprocessing
From raw documents to model-ready text
Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. What Tokenization Does
Tokenization converts text into units a model can process. A tokenizer may split a word into one token or several
subword pieces. For example, an uncommon technical term might be represented by multiple fragments rather
than a single token. Token IDs are vocabulary indices, not semantic scores. The embedding layer later maps these
IDs to vectors.
2. Why Subword Tokenization Is Useful
A vocabulary containing every possible word would be huge and would struggle with new names, spelling
variations, and technical terms. Subword methods balance vocabulary size with coverage. Common strings can
remain intact while rare words are decomposed into reusable pieces. This

overage. Common strings can
remain intact while rare words are decomposed into reusable pieces. This is especially useful for scientific writing,
code, product names, and multilingual text. Different model families use different tokenization algorithms and
vocabularies, so token counts can differ for the same passage.
3. Characters, Words, Tokens, and Chunks
Characters, words, model tokens, and retrieval chunks are different units. A 1,000-character passage is not
necessarily a fixed number of tokens. A chunk is a segment selected by an application for storage and retrieval; it
may be defined by characters, tokens, sentences, or document structure. When comparing chunking strategies,
record the actual method and parameters rather than assuming that a character limit corresponds to a universal
token count.

1. Inference in a Language Model
Inference is the process of using a trained model to produce an output for a given input. In an autoregressive
model, the system repeatedly predicts a distribution over the next token, selects a token according to a decoding
strategy, appends it to the context, and continues until a stopping condition is reached. The prompt and any
retrieved passages form part of the context available during generation.

scores into probabilities. The highest-probability token is not always selected: decoding settings may

controlled variation. Tokenization matters because the model selects token IDs, which are later decoded into
readable text.
3. Greedy Decoding and Sampling
Greedy decoding selects the token with the highest probability at each step. It is relatively deterministic but can
produce repetitive or generic output. Sampling draws from a probability distribution, allowing variation. Top-k
sampling restricts candidates to the k most likely tokens; nucleus or top-p sampling keeps a set whose cumulative
probability reaches a threshold. These methods trade predictability for diversity.
4. Temperature
Temperature adjusts the sharpness of the probability distribution before sampling. Lower temperatures make
high-scoring tokens more dominant; higher temperatures flatten the distribution and increase variation.

at a time. At each step, it produces a probability

decoding, top-k sampling, or nucleus (top-p) sampling, is used to select the next token.

The context window limits how much input and generated text can be handled in a single request. A request may

Pretraining exposes a model to a large collection of text or other data and optimizes it for a learning objective.
Many autoregressive language models learn to predict the next token given preceding tokens. Through this
objective, the model learns statistical patterns in language, facts represented in its data, and structures useful for
generating text. Pretraining is computationally expensive and the resulting model can still produce false statements

Transformers and Self-Attention
Core concepts behind modern language models
Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. Why Transformers Matter
A language model needs to interpret relationships between words and tokens. In the sentence “The animal did not
cross the road because it was tired,” the word “it” refers to the animal. A useful model must combine information
from different parts of the sequence. Earlier neural architectures often processed tokens sequentially, while the
Transformer architecture uses attention to relate tokens directly to one another. This makes parallel processing
during training practical and helps the model represent long-range dependencies.

4. Multi-Head Attention and Layers
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel. Different heads can learn different relationships,
such as local syntax, coreference, or broader semantic associations. Their outputs are combined and projected.
Transformer blocks typically also include feed-forward layers, residual connections, and layer normalization.
Stacking blocks allows representations to become progressively more contextual. The exact architecture differs
between encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder–decoder models.
5. A Small Example
Consider “A student opened the notebook because the lecture had started.” To interpret “the lecture,” the model
can attend to “started”; to interpret “the notebook,” it can attend to “opened” and “student.” These are illustrative
relationships, not guaranteed interpretations of particular attention heads. Attention weights are use

lationships, not guaranteed interpretations of particular attention heads. Attention weights are useful internal
computations, but they should not automatically be treated as complete explanations of a model’s reasoning.
6. Practical Strengths and Limits
Transformers support parallel training and flexible context mixing, but standard full self-attention has computational
and memory costs that grow approximately quadratically with sequence length. Long documents therefore require
careful context management, chunking, or specialized attention methods. Attention also does not guarantee factual
correctness: a model may produce a fluent answer that is unsupported by its input.

Tokenization and Text Preprocessing
From raw documents to model-ready text
Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. What Tokenization Does
Tokenization converts text into units a model can process. A tokenizer may split a word into one token or several
subword pieces. For example, an uncommon technical term might be represented by multiple fragments rather
than a single token. Token IDs are vocabulary indices, not semantic scores. The embedding layer later maps these
IDs to vectors.
2. Why Subword Tokenization Is Useful
A vocabulary containing every possible word would be huge and would struggle with new names, spelling
variations, and technical terms. Subword methods balance vocabulary size with coverage. Common strings can
remain intact while rare words are decomposed into reusable pieces. This

overage. Common strings can
remain intact while rare words are decomposed into reusable pieces. This is especially useful for scientific writing,
code, product names, and multilingual text. Different model families use different tokenization algorithms and
vocabularies, so token counts can differ for the same passage.
3. Characters, Words, Tokens, and Chunks
Characters, words, model tokens, and retrieval chunks are different units. A 1,000-character passage is not
necessarily a fixed number of tokens. A chunk is a segment selected by an application for storage and retrieval; it
may be defined by characters, tokens, sentences, or document structure. When comparing chunking strategies,
record the actual method and parameters rather than assuming that a character limit corresponds to a universal
token count.

reading-order problems. A preprocessing pipeline shoul

e quality of the text entering the pipeline.
6. How Tokenization Affects Retrieval
Embedding models generally accept token sequences with model-specific limits. Very long input may be truncated
or rejected. A chunk that is too large may exceed the embedding model’s input limit; a chunk that is too small may
omit context needed to interpret a term. Token counts also affect latency and cost for hosted model APIs. The right
chunk size should be tested against representative questions, not selected from a universal rule.

LLMs are typically trained in multiple stages. The first stage, pretraining, involves training the model
on a very large, diverse corpus of text using the next-token prediction objective. This stage requires
enormous computational resources and is where the model acquires most of its general knowledge
and language ability.
The second stage, often called fine-tuning or instruction tuning, involves further training the model on
smaller, curated datasets of instructions and desired responses, teaching the model to follow user
instructions more reliably.
A third stage, commonly Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), uses human
preference data to further align model outputs with what humans consider helpful, honest, and
harmless, by training a reward model and using it to fine-tune the LLM's behavior.

4. Fine-Tuning Versus RAG
Fine-tuning changes model parameters; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant external
passages at answer time. Fine-tuning can shape behavior, style, or task performance. RAG is often more
convenient when facts change frequently or answers must cite a private document collection. The approaches can

Transformers and Self-Attention
Core concepts behind modern language models
Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. Why Transformers Matter
A language model needs to interpret relationships between words and tokens. In the sentence “The animal did not
cross the road because it was tired,” the word “it” refers to the animal. A useful model must combine information
from different parts of the sequence. Earlier neural architectures often processed tokens sequentially, while the
Transformer architecture uses attention to relate tokens directly to one another. This makes parallel processing
during training practical and helps the model represent long-range dependencies.
2. Tokens, Embeddings, and Positions
Text is first converted into tokens. A token may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation,

ions
Text is first converted into tokens. A token may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text unit.
Each token ID is mapped to a vector called an embedding. Since attention alone does not inherently encode token
order, positional information is added to the token representations. The resulting vectors carry both lexical
information and a signal about where each token appears in the sequence.
3. The Self-Attention Operation
Self-attention creates query, key, and value vectors from each token representation. A query represents what a
token is looking for; keys represent what other tokens offer for matching; values carry the information that can be
combined. Similarity scores between queries and keys are scaled and normalized with softmax. The normalized
weights are used to compute a weighted combination of values. In simplified notation, Attention(Q,K,V) =
softmax(QKn / (cid:214)dn)V. The scaling term helps keep scores in a useful range as the key dimension grows.

Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel. Different heads can learn different relationships,
such as local syntax, coreference, or broader semantic associations. Their outputs are combined and projected.

1. What Tokenization Does
Tokenization converts text into units a model can process. A tokenizer may split a word into one token or several
subword pieces. For example, an uncommon technical term might be represented by multiple fragments rather

1. What Is a Context Window?
A context window is the amount of tokenized input and output a model can process in a request. Depending on the
model and API, the limit may count the system prompt, user message, retrieved passages, conversation history,
and generated response. A large context window does not mean that every included detail will be used equally
well.

A RAG prompt has several competing uses for tokens: instructions, the question, retrieved evidence, conversation
history, and answer generation. If the combined request exceeds the limit, the API may reject it or the application
may need to truncate content. Truncation can remove exactl

al parametric knowledge.

data up to a specific cutoff date.

Embedding models generally accept token sequences with model-specific limits. Very long input may be truncated

An embedding is a numerical vector produced from text, images, or another input. Text embeddings are designed

From raw documents to model-ready text
Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. What Tokenization Does
Tokenization converts text into units a model can process. A tokenizer may split a word into one token or several
subword pieces. For example, an uncommon technical term might be represented by multiple fragments rather
than a single token. Token IDs are vocabulary indices, not semantic scores. The embedding layer later maps these
IDs to vectors.
2. Why Subword Tokenization Is Useful

Pretraining exposes a model to a large collection of text or other data and optimizes it for a learning objective.

LLMs are typically trained in multiple stages. The first stage, pretraining, involves training the model

The second stage, often called fine-tuning or instruction tuning, involves further training the model on
smaller, curated datasets of instructions and desired responses, teaching the model to follow user

A Large Language Model (LLM) is a type of neural network trained on massive amounts of text data

objective, the model learns statistical patterns in language, facts represented in its data, and structures useful for
generating text. Pretraining is computationally expensive and the resulting model can still produce false statements

on.

1. What Tokenization Does
Tokenization converts text into units a model can process. A tokenizer may split a word into one token or several
subword pieces. For example, an uncommon technical term might be represented by multiple fragments rather
than a single token. Token IDs are vocabulary indices, not semantic scores. The embedding layer later maps these
IDs to vectors.
2. Why Subword Tokenization Is Useful
A vocabulary containing every possible word would be huge and would struggle with new names, spelling
variations, and technical terms. Subword methods balance vocabulary size with coverage. Common strings can
remain intact while rare words are decomposed into reusable pieces. This

overage. Common strings can

code, product names, and multilingual text. Different model families use different tokenization algorithms and
vocabularies, so token counts can differ for the same passage.

necessarily a fixed number of tokens. A chunk is a segment selected by an application for storage and retrieval; it
may be defined by characters, tokens, sentences, or document structure. When comparing chunking strategies,
record the actual method and parameters rather than assuming that a character limit corresponds to a universal

Inference is the process of using a trained model to produce an output for a given input. In an autoregressive
model, the system repeatedly predicts a distribution over the next token, selects a token according to a decoding
strategy, appends it to the context, and continues until a stopping condition is reached. The prompt and any
retrieved passages form part of the context available during generation.

produce repetitive or generic output. Sampling draws from a probability distribution, allowing variation. Top-k
sampling restricts candidates to the k most likely tokens; nucleus or top-p sampling keeps a set whose cumulative
probability reaches a threshold. These methods trade predictability for diversity.

How Large Language Models Work
1. What Is a Large Language Model
A Large Language Model (LLM) is a type of neural network trained on massive amounts of text data
to predict the next word, or more precisely the next token, in a sequence. Despite this relatively
simple training objective, LLMs learn to capture grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and even some
limited problem-solving ability purely from statistical patterns in the training data.

mechanism called self-attention, which allows the model to weigh the relevance of every other token
in a sequence when processing a given token, regardless of distance between them.

A Large Language Model (LLM) is a type of neural network trained on massive amounts of text data
to predict the next word, or more precisely the next token, in a sequence. Despite this relatively

Fine-tuning changes model parameters; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant external

A Large Language Model (LLM) is a type of neural network trained on massive amounts of text data
to predict the next word, or more precisely the next token, in a sequence. Despite this relatively

Core concepts behind modern language models
Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. Why Transformers Matter
A language model needs to interpret relationships between words and tokens. In the sentence “The animal did not
cross the road because it was tired,” the word “it” refers to the animal. A useful model must combine information
from different parts of the sequence. Earlier neural architectures often processed tokens sequentially, while the
Transformer architecture uses attention to relate tokens directly to one another. This makes parallel processing
during training practical and helps the model represent long-range dependencies.

Text is first converted into tokens. A token may be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text unit.
Each token ID is mapped to a vector called an embedding. Since attention alone does not inherently encode token
order, positional information is added to the token representations. The resulting vectors carry both lexical
information and a signal about where each token appears in the sequence.
3. The Self-Attention Operation
Self-attention creates query, key, and value vectors from each token representation. A query represents what a
token is looking for; keys represent what other tokens offer for matching; values carry the information that can be
combined. Similarity scores between queries and keys are scaled and normalized with softmax. The normalized
weights are used to compute a weighted combination of values. In simplified notation, Attention(Q,K,V) =

Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel. Different heads can learn different relationships,

1. What Tokenization Does
Tokenization converts text into units a model can process. A tokenizer may split a word into one token or several
subword pieces. For example, an uncommon technical term might be represented by multiple fragments rather
than a single token. Token IDs are vocabulary indices, not semantic scores. The embedding layer later maps these
IDs to vectors.
2. Why Subword Tokenization Is Useful
A vocabulary containing every possible word would be huge and would struggle with new names, spelling

necessarily a fixed number of tokens. A chunk is a segment selected by an application for storage and retrieval; it

LLMs are typically trained in multiple stages. The first stage, pretraining, involves training the model
on a very large, diverse corpus of text using the next-token prediction objective. This stage requires
enormous computational resources and is where the model acquires most of its general knowledge
and language ability.
The second stage, often called fine-tuning or instruction tuning, involves further training the model on
smaller, curated datasets of instructions and desired responses, teaching the model to follow user
instructions more reliably.
A third stage, commonly Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), uses human
preference data to further align model outputs with what humans consider helpful, honest, and
harmless, by training a reward model and using it to fine-tune the LLM's behavior.

1. What Is a Large Language Model
A Large Language Model (LLM) is a type of neural network trained on massive amounts of text data

4. Fine-Tuning Versus RAG
Fine-tuning changes model parameters; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant external
passages at answer time. Fine-tuning can shape behavior, style, or task performance. RAG is often more
convenient when facts change frequently or answers must cite a private document collection. The approaches can
be combined, but they solve different problems. If a system must answer questions about newly uploaded PDFs,
retrieval is usually the first mechanism to evaluate before considering fine-tuning.
5. Data Quality and Evaluation
Training examples should be relevant, consistent, legally usable, and representative of real use. Separate training
data from evaluation data to avoid measuring memorization. Evaluate not only average accuracy but also edge
cases, unsupported questions, format compliance, and regressions. Keep a baseline model and configuration so
changes can be compared fairly.

Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. What Is an Embedding?
An embedding is a numerical vector produced from text, images, or another input. Text embeddings are designed
so that useful semantic relationships can be represented geometrically. Passages about related ideas may have
vectors that are close under a chosen similarity or distance measure. An embedding is not a human-readable
definition and its individual dimensions usually do not correspond to simple concepts.
2. Creating Document and Query Vectors
A retrieval pipeline typically splits documents into chunks, creates an embedding for each chunk, and stores the
vector with the chunk text and metadata. At query time, the user’s question is embedded using a compatib

ed into tokens, which are numerical
representations of subword units. Tokenization algorithms such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) break
text into frequently occurring chunks, which may be whole words, parts of words, or even individual
characters for rare terms.
This subword approach allows the model to handle a fixed-size vocabulary while still representing
rare or unseen words by combining smaller known subword units, avoiding the need for an infinitely
large vocabulary.
3. Embeddings and Self-Attention
Each token is converted into a dense numerical vector called an embedding, which captures
semantic meaning in a high-dimensional space. Words with similar meanings tend to have
embeddings that are close together in this space.
The self-attention mechanism then computes, for each token, a weighted combination of all other
tokens in the input, using three learned projections called Query, Key, and Value vectors. This allows
the model to determine which parts of the input are most relevant

Key Takeaways
Embeddings provide a geometric representation that makes semantic search possible. Similarity scores rank
candidates; they do not prove that a passage is correct, complete, or sufficient to answer the question.

1. Why Transformers Matter
A language model needs to interpret relationships between words and tokens. In the sentence “The animal did not
cross the road because it was tired,” the word “it” refers to the animal. A useful model must combine information
from different parts of the sequence. Earlier neural architectures often processed tokens sequentially, while the
Transformer architecture uses attention to relate tokens directly to one another. This makes parallel processing
during training practical and helps the model represent long-range dependencies.

4. Multi-Head Attention and Layers
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel. Different heads can learn different relationships,
such as local syntax, coreference, or broader semantic associations. Their outputs are combined and projected.

4. Fine-Tuning Versus RAG
Fine-tuning changes model parameters; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant external
passages at answer time. Fine-tuning can shape behavior, style, or task performance. RAG is often more
convenient when facts change frequently or answers must cite a private document collection. The approaches can
be combined, but they solve different problems. If a system must answer questions about newly uploaded PDFs,
